items.stem: Which choice best paraphrases the point made in the sentence “To address this problem, archivists attached explanations to uncertain terms rather than silently replacing them with modern equivalents”?
choices: The archivists preserved questionable expressions and explained them instead of secretly changing them into contemporary language.
The archivists replaced unfamiliar expressions with modern terms so that every search would produce more matches.
The archivists removed uncertain words from the diaries because explanations would make the records less readable.

items.stimulus: When the Harbor Museum began digitizing its collection of sailors' diaries, staff expected the work to make the records easier to search without changing what they meant. Yet many entries used tide names, nicknames, and abbreviations that only made sense within particular crews, so a searchable transcript could be more legible than the original while being less informative. To address this problem, archivists attached explanations to uncertain terms rather than silently replacing them with modern equivalents. They also preserved crossings-out and awkward grammar, because those features sometimes revealed whether a sentence had been written during an event or reconstructed later. This caution slowed the project: users had to consult notes, and some searches returned fewer apparent matches than a simplified transcript would have. The loss was partly offset by a discovery: clusters of repeated nicknames and tide expressions allowed researchers to link diaries whose authors had never identified one another. Thus, the archive's usefulness came not from removing ambiguity but from making the locations and limits of ambiguity visible. Digitization, in this case, did not turn messy testimony into neutral data; it gave readers a more accountable way to encounter its messiness.

To test whether obstruction or location explained the pattern, the team compared paired plots—one cleared and one partially obstructed—and sampled water at several downstream points. Cleared plots showed lower sediment levels near channel mouths but higher concentrations farther away, whereas obstructed plots retained more coarse material locally and released less fine sediment downstream. Because the researchers measured both the channel and downstream water, they treated “success” as reducing marsh-wide sediment redistribution, not simply making an individual channel look clean.

This definition changed the interpretation: a visually tidy channel could signal that sediment had merely been exported, while an untidy one could be holding material in place. The team cautioned that roots and reeds were not universally beneficial; after unusually high tides, dense debris could divert flow toward banks. For restoration planners, the study therefore recommends varying obstacles and monitoring where sediment goes, rather than judging a project by the speed of local clearing alone.

items.stimulus:
In the dry valleys of northern Chile, the silverleaf shrub survives by storing water in its thick leaves. During prolonged drought, the leaves curl inward, reducing the surface exposed to the air. Earlier researchers thought this curling was simply a passive response to dehydration.

Botanist Lina Ortega noticed that curled leaves also shaded the shrub’s developing buds. To test this observation, she tied some leaves open while leaving neighboring plants untouched. After six weeks, the open leaves had lost more water, and their buds were more likely to be damaged by intense sunlight. The result suggested that curling served two purposes: conserving water and shielding developing flowers.

Ortega next examined whether the curling mattered after the rainy season, when water was plentiful. Plants whose leaves had curled produced flowers at roughly the same rate as plants whose leaves had been kept flat. Thus, curling appeared to be useful chiefly during drought, when both water loss and sun damage posed serious risks.

items.stem: Which choice best paraphrases the first paragraph?
choices: The researchers expected cleared channels to retain sediment, but they found that strong currents in those channels transported sediment more efficiently than the channels containing roots and reeds.

items.stimulus:
Researchers at Marrow Marsh expected restored channels to export accumulated sediment faster after tidal flushing because unobstructed water should move more freely. Instead, sediment accumulation declined most in plots where volunteers left tangled roots and fallen reeds in place. The result did not make flow irrelevant: strong currents removed loose material quickly, but in cleared plots they also carried fragments downstream, where those fragments broke apart and settled in slower water.

To test whether obstruction or location explained the pattern, the team compared paired plots—one cleared and one partially obstructed—and sampled water at several downstream points. Cleared plots showed lower sediment levels near channel mouths but higher concentrations farther away, whereas obstructed plots retained more coarse material locally and released less fine sediment downstream. Because the researchers measured both the channel and downstream water, they treated “success” as reducing marsh-wide sediment redistribution, not simply making an individual channel look clean.

This definition changed the interpretation: a visually tidy channel could signal that sediment had merely been exported, while an untidy one could be holding material in place. The team cautioned that roots and reeds were not universally beneficial; after unusually high tides, dense debris could divert flow toward banks. For restoration planners, the study therefore recommends varying obstacles and monitoring where sediment goes, rather than judging a project by the speed of local clearing alone.

items.stem: Why did Venn begin comparing the timing and location of moisture rather than relying on the amount measured immediately after fog?
choices: The lichen mats were found to hold droplets only briefly, confirming that surface storage was their main function.
The unexpectedly low surface reading in dense plots suggested that water might have been redirected rather than lost, challenging her original model.
The three foggy summers produced too little moisture for her to compare dense plots with bare ground.
The team had already established that shallow-rooted grasses survived better in dense plots than in cleared plots.
items.stimulus:
Along a dry southern coast, ecologist Mara Venn studied “fog gardens,” patches of lichen that intercept moisture from low clouds. She initially assumed that lichens mattered only by holding droplets near the surface until plant roots could use them. However, after three unusually foggy summers, dense plots showed less water in their top centimeter immediately after fog than sparse plots and bare ground did. Because this pattern seemed to contradict her model, Venn began comparing the timing and location of moisture rather than its immediate surface amount.

Chemical tracers revealed that lichen filaments channeled droplets through cracks in the soil crust into layers two to three centimeters below the surface, where evaporation was slower. Thus, dense plots lost water from the surface quickly but retained more water below the surface for several days. Young grasses beside dense mats grew slowly at first because their shallow roots reached little of the diverted water, while shrubs with deeper roots later had higher survival there. The same measurement—a dry upper layer—therefore signaled a short-term disadvantage to one plant and a longer-term benefit to another.

To test whether the mats themselves caused this pattern, the team removed them from paired plots while leaving the soil and slope unchanged. After light rains, grasses germinated more abundantly in cleared plots, but during a month without rain, seedlings there died at nearly twice the rate observed among grasses in intact plots. Venn concluded that fog gardens function less as reservoirs than as routing systems, changing where and when fog water becomes accessible. She recommended preserving patches with mixed lichen densities: dense mats can sustain deep-rooted plants through dry intervals, while open patches allow shallow-rooted plants to capitalize on brief surface wetness.

Urban tree programs are usually judged by survival, but a study broadened that evaluation by examining whether trees also developed canopies and cooled their surroundings.
items.stimulus:
Researchers who evaluate urban tree-planting programs often begin with the simplest measure: the percentage of saplings alive after two years. In dry neighborhoods, however, a living sapling can cast almost no shade if it has developed a sparse canopy, while a dead sapling may reflect a planting site rather than a species’ inability to grow. To distinguish these possibilities, a team followed 240 saplings in three kinds of sites—city-irrigated lots, community-managed plots, and plots receiving little organized care. The researchers recorded survival, canopy spread, nearby surface temperatures, watering logs, and interviews with people responsible for maintenance.

The team expected city-irrigated lots to produce both the highest survival and the greatest cooling because those lots received water on a regular schedule. Instead, community-managed plots had somewhat lower survival but, among their surviving trees, broader canopies and greater local cooling. Interviews suggested that volunteers concentrated water on fewer saplings during heat waves, whereas city crews watered every sapling according to a fixed schedule, even when some sites still retained moisture. Satellite images confirmed that cooling was strongest in clusters surrounding the largest surviving trees, reinforcing the measurements taken at individual sites.

The findings do not make survival counts irrelevant: those counts reveal whether a program is losing plants broadly and allow comparisons across planting seasons. They do show, however, that survival alone answers a narrower question than planners often assume. The team therefore recommends reporting survival alongside canopy development and cooling rather than replacing one measure with another. Such paired accounting could shift funding from distributing more seedlings toward supporting maintenance practices, because the program’s practical success depends not only on keeping trees alive but also on producing usable shade where people live.

items.stem: What did the interviews most directly help the researchers explain?

items.stimulus:
Researchers who evaluate urban tree-planting programs often begin with the simplest measure: the percentage of saplings alive after two years. In dry neighborhoods, however, a living sapling can cast almost no shade if it has developed a sparse canopy, while a dead sapling may reflect a planting site rather than a species’ inability to grow. To distinguish these possibilities, a team followed 240 saplings in three kinds of sites—city-irrigated lots, community-managed plots, and plots receiving little organized care. The researchers recorded survival, canopy spread, nearby surface temperatures, watering logs, and interviews with people responsible for maintenance.

The team expected city-irrigated lots to produce both the highest survival and the greatest cooling because those lots received water on a regular schedule. Instead, community-managed plots had somewhat lower survival but, among their surviving trees, broader canopies and greater local cooling. Interviews suggested that volunteers concentrated water on fewer saplings during heat waves, whereas city crews watered every sapling according to a fixed schedule, even when some sites still retained moisture. Satellite images confirmed that cooling was strongest in clusters surrounding the largest surviving trees, reinforcing the measurements taken at individual sites.

The findings do not make survival counts irrelevant: those counts reveal whether a program is losing plants broadly and allow comparisons across planting seasons. They do show, however, that survival alone answers a narrower question than planners often assume. The team therefore recommends reporting survival alongside canopy development and cooling rather than replacing one measure with another. Such paired accounting could shift funding from distributing more seedlings toward supporting maintenance practices, because the program’s practical success depends not only on keeping trees alive but also on producing usable shade where people live.

items.stem: Which choice best paraphrases the ecologists' comparison and measurements described in the first paragraph?
choices: They compared crusted and bare soil to determine how each affected both the initial entry of water and its later persistence.
They examined several kinds of desert organisms to determine which one could absorb the greatest amount of water.

items.stimulus:
On desert ground, a thin living layer called a biological soil crust can cover the spaces between shrubs. Mosses, algae, and other small organisms bind soil particles into this layer. Though dry crusts can look inert, they may influence what happens to water when rain arrives. To test this effect, ecologists compared crust-covered soil with nearby bare soil and measured both the amount of water entering the ground and the amount remaining there later.

During the first minute of simulated rain, crusted soil took in less water than bare soil. Yet after twenty-four hours, the crusted samples held more water. In outdoor plots, where showers arrived as several pulses rather than one, crusted soil produced less runoff overall, especially when later pulses followed a dry interval. Researchers think the crust's rough surface initially slows water, while tiny channels and organic material later help distribute and hold it.

Foot traffic altered this pattern by breaking the crust into patches and exposing loose soil. In plots with intact crust, water retention increased over the first three years after protection, then leveled off; partially damaged plots improved more slowly. The findings suggest that crusts do not act simply as sponges: their value lies in changing both the speed at which water enters soil and the length of time it remains available.

items.stimulus:
On the first morning after her mother’s funeral, Lena climbed to the apartment roof to sort through the things no one had touched in years. Before her illness, her mother had asked Lena to clear the roof, but Lena had always postponed the task. Among the boxes, Lena found her grandfather’s hand-built shadow theater. Its painted panels showed a moon, a bridge, and a row of crooked houses, although one corner had split and the hinges were rusted.

As a child, Lena had watched her grandfather move paper figures behind the panels, and she still remembered the audience’s laughter from those evenings. Although the memory made the theater precious, its warped wood and missing screen convinced her that it could not be used again. When she lifted the rear panel, however, she discovered a narrow strip of blue cloth hidden inside it. The strip bore chalk marks that corresponded to the angles of the panels. The marks did not tell her what the theater had been for, but they persuaded her to measure it before discarding it.

By dusk, Lena had discovered that the panels were designed to fold around a single lantern rather than stand as a fixed screen. Tomas, the neighbor who had once helped her grandfather, told Lena that the theater had been used during neighborhood blackouts, when people gathered in the courtyard to watch improvised stories. His account made Lena see the theater as both a keepsake and a device repeatedly altered for shared use. Rather than rebuild it into its original form, she fitted the loose hinges with removable pins. When the evening wind made the painted shadows waver across the rooftop door, Lena left the panels in place, unfinished but ready to be changed again.

In 1912, curator Liora Sen inherited a museum collection of household tools whose arrangement had changed little in decades. Most museums then grouped objects by material, date, or place of origin, but Sen organized her galleries according to the task each object performed. Her first gallery placed a carpenter’s plane beside a baker’s rolling pin because both altered a surface through pressure. Sen believed that such pairings would make visitors notice actions shared by objects that looked unrelated.

To make those choices less arbitrary, Sen excluded objects whose uses were uncertain, even when their craftsmanship was exceptional. She also commissioned labels that began with verbs such as “measure” and “smooth” instead of dates or makers’ names. Critics praised the labels for directing attention to activity, but accused Sen of erasing the social differences between the people who had used the tools.

Later scholars described this revision as a retreat from Sen’s original experiment, yet a surviving floor plan shows that the panels were positioned as bridges between galleries rather than replacements for them. Sen’s experiment therefore did not reject historical order altogether; it treated chronology as one interpretive tool to be used after visitors had considered what objects enabled people to do.
